headline: World Gold Council's John Reid outlines multi-factor drivers behind gold's 65% surge in 2025 including central bank buying, EM retail demand, and ETF inflows
reasoning: Reid explains that the unprecedented gold rally was driven by three converging forces: central banks doubling purchases from ~500 to ~1,000 tons annually from 2022, strong retail demand from emerging markets (India, China, Turkey), and a late-cycle awakening by Western investors through ETFs in mid-2025. ETF investors swung from marginal net sellers in 2024 to buying 800 tons in 2025, which was the largest year-on-year demand change. All forms of investment demand — ETFs, physical bars and coins, OTC — were active simultaneously, creating an unusually broad-based rally. The 65% US dollar return in 2025 compared to a long-run average of 8-9% per annum was described as extraordinary and unsustainable at that pace.
quote: It really I think was a combination of factors that were coming together. We've seen the central banking community which have been buying gold since 2010. Back in 2022 it doubled its purchases from about a tenth of the market to about 20% of the market. So from 500 tons to about a thousand tons. So that really set up the beginnings of the move higher in gold. Then we saw tremendous investment from various emerging market countries. Retail investors in India, in China, in Turkey and other countries from time to time. Buying gold for mainly domestic economic and political reasons. And then finally Western investors woke up to what was going on perhaps in the middle of 2025 and started participating in the rise that we've seen in the price.
episode_title: Weekend Edition: Gold - safe haven or speculative investment?

headline: Higher oil prices are currently bad for gold demand because Western equity markets are not panicking; a shift in equity sentiment would quickly revive safe-haven gold buying
reasoning: Reid argues that gold's safe-haven role is conditional on equity market distress. Currently, with US and Western equity markets broadly ignoring the Iran conflict and higher oil prices, there is no widespread fear driving investors to gold. Higher oil prices raise inflation and rate expectations, which discourage ETF gold purchases and incentivise profit-taking. However, if rising oil prices eventually pressure equities, Western investors can pivot to gold very rapidly, as demonstrated in previous crises. The missing ingredient for safe-haven demand is a genuine equity market correction.
quote: Whilst there is a lack of fear, particularly in Western equity markets, then on balance, I'd say higher oil prices are probably bad for gold demand and therefore likely bad for prices, as we've seen since the Iranian conflict started. If we get to the stage, though, where this higher oil prices and moves in the treasury market, et cetera, start to affect sentiment towards equities, then that can turn around quickly. Western investors, when they are worried, can turn to gold very quickly.
episode_title: Weekend Edition: Gold - safe haven or speculative investment?

headline: Gold mine supply constrained at ~0.7% growth per annum over last decade; higher prices causing some restart of operations in Canada and Western Australia but no rapid supply response
reasoning: Reid explains that gold mine production grows at only about 0.7% per annum over the last decade, far slower than the price signal would suggest. Mines are not factories — they have finite resources and eventually shut down, requiring continuous new project discovery. Higher prices are causing some restarts of previously discontinued operations in Canada and Western Australia, but big new projects are scarce. This supply constraint means that a surge in investment demand (such as the extra ~1,000 tons in 2025) cannot be met by new supply and instead prices out price-elastic demand (jewellery), pushing prices higher. The annual stock increase is only about 1.6-1.7% of the existing above-ground stock of ~220,000 tons.
quote: Is that mine production growth accelerating? And the margin it is, these higher prices are causing restarts of previously discontinued operations in Canada, in Western Australia, in some other countries as well. But there is a shortage of big projects out there. And as I remind people, a gold mine is not a factory. It doesn't last forever. It has a finite resource. When you mined all that gold, that mine shuts down. So you've got to keep finding new projects, new mines to keep mine production steady. The rate of mine production growth over the last decade has been about 0.7% per annum.
episode_title: Weekend Edition: Gold - safe haven or speculative investment?

headline: Tether buying ~80 tons of gold for stablecoin reserves highlights gold's role as ultimate protection against debasement even within the crypto ecosystem
reasoning: Reid notes that Tether, which issues a USD-backed stablecoin and is central to the crypto ecosystem, purchased approximately 80 tons of gold in 2025 for its general reserves — not for a specific gold token. Out of a 5,000-ton market this is small but not insignificant. quote: The interesting thing we have seen, though, is Tether, which issues a US dollar back stablecoin and is really one of the key ingredients of the crypto ecosphere. They have been buying gold, and it's not for their gold token. It's actually for their general reserves for the US dollar stablecoin. And they bought about 80 tons of gold last year, I think is the number. Now, out of a 5,000 ton market, that's small, but it's not insignificant. And on the basis that Tether has about $180 billion US dollars worth of stablecoins issued, I think it's very funny that something at the center of the crypto universe is recognizing that gold is the ultimate protection against debasement. And in a way, it actually undercuts the argument for Bitcoin to a degree.
episode_title: Weekend Edition: Gold - safe haven or speculative investment?

headline: Gold's 2026 correction driven by Iran conflict triggering ETF outflows, central bank selling, and profit-taking amid higher rate expectations

ETF investors added about 800 tons in 2025, and year to date, they're more or less flat. So that's a big change year on year. So ETF investors buying less gold, we're seeing less demand from bar and coin investors as well. And obviously, high prices are seeing jewelry demand for year on year as well. headline: Central banks and long-term investors reducing US Treasury and developed-market bond exposure, redirecting capital to gold as a reserve asset

headline: Gold's inflation-hedge credentials are nuanced: it works best against monetary inflation and stagflation, not rising CPI driven by commodity prices
reasoning: Reid clarifies the distinction between gold as a monetary inflation hedge versus a CPI hedge. Gold performs best when central banks are expanding their balance sheets (printing money), as seen during the GFC and early COVID. In a conventional inflationary episode driven by commodity prices, commodities themselves (especially oil) are better hedges. Gold also performs well in stagflationary environments where central banks fail to raise rates adequately. But if central banks respond correctly by hiking rates, gold underperforms versus commodities. The nomination of Kevin Walsh as Fed chair, with his known preference for a smaller balance sheet, was cited as a trigger for the January 2026 correction.
quote: Gold holds its value and actually delivers real returns over the long term. In terms of inflation, it works best as a hedge against monetary inflation. And what I mean by that is central banks printing money. So if you look at when central banks have printed money during the global financial crisis, during the early stages of COVID, gold performed really well. When inflation comes along, it's less good a hedge. So when CPI is going up, then the better hedges is coming through from exposure to the commodities that usually driving inflation, and that kind of means oil.
episode_title: Weekend Edition: Gold - safe haven or speculative investment?

headline: Longer-term structural case for gold intact driven by US credibility concerns, unsustainable developed-market debt trajectories, and high-net-worth capital reallocation

We want to think about not just this quarter's performance, but our children, our grandchildren, and making sure that they will be financially secure. So it doesn't take a lot of movement of some of these really large pools of capital towards gold to make a big difference.

headline: Norway's cash-flow tax model for gas is seen as superior to PRRT but requires government co-investment and upfront risk-sharing
reasoning: Vass highlights Norway's resource tax system as a frequently cited model, noting it is similar in spirit to the PRRT but avoids the cost-base uplift problem. Under Norway's cash-flow tax, the government co-invests — paying out a share of losses in bad years and recouping a share of profits in good years — meaning revenue moves more directly with commodity prices. The downside is that taxpayers bear risk in loss years. Norway's approach has generated a sovereign wealth fund of over $1.6 trillion USD, no government debt, free healthcare, free university and large pensions. However, transitioning Australia to such a system would require compensating existing projects for their $280 billion cost-base deductions, potentially costing tens of billions of dollars.
quote: The Norway system is different to the way this transition works in that the government is a co-investor both through direct equity. But they also have something called a cash flow tax, which is whenever a company makes a loss, the government pays them a certain percentage of that loss out in money. And then when they make a gain, the government then takes up money back in. And so that's analogous to the PRRT. But without this uplift factor and cost-based issue. So it's seen as more appealing because when the price goes up, you see the revenue straight away... The current existing stock of deductions under the PRRT is about $280 billion. And even if it's a fraction of that, it'd be an interesting question for government where they wanted to pay out tens of billions of dollars to gas companies as part of a transition to tax and more.

headline: PRRT cost base of $280bn means gas companies unlikely to pay meaningful tax before early 2030s despite high prices
reasoning: Vass explains that the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT) allows companies to carry forward and uplift unrecouped capital costs, meaning that until the cumulative cost base is paid off, no PRRT is owed. The current stock of deductions is approximately $280 billion, which is why despite high gas prices, PRRT revenue has remained flat at around $1.4 billion per year. The Callahan Review in 2017 projected revenue would meaningfully kick up in the 2030s; Vass thinks windfalls since then may have brought that forward to the early 2030s, but it is unlikely to occur before 2030. Two key structural problems are: (1) the historically generous uplift rate of government bond rate plus 15% inflated the cost base, and (2) internal gas transfer pricing may have understated the taxable value of gas, further limiting revenue.
quote: So that's partly the timing you should be talked about before when those large cost bases that have built over time. So even though they tweak the uplift rate lower, the pool or the size of those cost bases remain. I think the latest numbers put them at about two hundred and eighty billion dollars that we're still kind of chewing through. So that's one reason why you haven't seen over the four year forecast and uptick in PRRT... I think in the Callahan Review in 2017, they were projecting 2030s would be when the revenue really kicks up. We've probably had a few windfalls since then. So maybe instead of mid 2030s, it might be early 2030s. But it's really hard to know. It definitely doesn't look like it's going to be before 2030 based on the latest budget.

headline: Switching to a royalty-based regime for offshore gas would raise revenue sooner but would reduce investment at the margin
reasoning: Vass notes that onshore gas and resources are taxed via state royalties from the first unit extracted, while offshore gas falls under the Commonwealth PRRT regime. A royalty system offers simpler, more visible, and earlier revenue, but economists regard it as distortionary because it raises the investment hurdle rate regardless of profitability, potentially discouraging marginal projects. The tradeoff is between a simpler system with certain early revenue versus a more complex system that theoretically maximises long-run production and tax revenue. Vass says there is no free lunch — any move to royalties would mean less investment at the margin.
quote: There is a trade off that I can see in the appeal of the royalty. But it does leave money on the table and it also distorts or dissuades investment. And so if you are someone who wants to kind of maximize production and maximize the size of the pie, it does have an impact on it... if we go down that royalty route, it does mean less investment at the margin going forward.

headline: Gas transfer pricing and inflated uplift rates are the two main structural flaws in the PRRT that need addressing
reasoning: Vass identifies two principal deficiencies in the PRRT. First, the original uplift rate of government bond rate plus 15% was too generous, inflating cost bases to a level that may never be paid off on some projects. The 2019 reform reduced this to bond rate plus 5%, but the legacy stock remains. Second, the internal transfer pricing used to value gas at the point of extraction — rather than at the point of export — may have allowed companies to understate the taxable value of the commodity, limiting their PRRT liability. Vass also argues that better public data from the ATO or Treasury on the trajectory of the cost base would help inform the policy debate.
quote: There are two main issues with the BRT that have been documented and a little bit of actions taken, but maybe more can happen. Firstly, it's how you set that up. If right. It was government bond plus 50 percent. And the stock of those things still exist. Whether we want to go back and address the size of those things. We've made sure it's going to be a smaller stock going forward. And then the second one is a gas transfer pricing, how we calculate the value of that gas and how we're being too, too generous. They're the two main things. And then I think it would be complemented really well in the debate. And to inform policymakers having better data on how we're tracking in the public domain.

headline: Domestic gas reservation is analogous to an export tax but benefits consumers rather than government revenue

But there's a slight difference in that in an export tax world, the government reaps the tax benefits and by implication, the rest of the country. Whereas in the gas reservation world, it's actually the consumers, the domestic consumers of gas who read the benefits of that system. And I suppose it's not clear why the domestic consumers of gas should be subsidised relative to Australians more broadly.
